decision: Do our tiers and price points hold together, where does revenue come from, and what would a price change do to it?
limitations: It does the arithmetic on the tiers you enter: MRR, ARPU, revenue mix, price steps, the anchor and margin. It can't tell you what buyers will pay, which value metric fits, or how many customers a price change will lose.

A what-if counts every customer on a tier as average. A break-even is how many customers a tier can lose or must add, not a forecast of how many will. A customer who moves tier is counted at the average of the tier they join.
The 1.5x weak-anchor line and the 1.6x ARPU line are AAJ's rules of thumb, not published benchmarks. For a product with no customers, the mix is your estimate, so every figure is an assumption.

Seats, usage, annual share and cost are averages you supply for each tier. MRR spreads a yearly payment over twelve months, so it is not cash received. The engine does not model churn over time, taxes or currencies.
review: Whoever owns pricing checks the tier prices, the customer mix and the per-tier averages, marked as estimates if projected, and owns the customers-lost number in any what-if. The finance lead cross-checks the blended ARPU against CAC and payback in unit-economics before any price goes live.
